strengths: Addresses a clear and well-motivated gap: existing multimodal browsing benchmarks (e.g., MMSearch) can be solved with shallow workflows relying on high-recall image search plus surrounding text, and this paper's Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation curation targets genuinely multimodal, fine-grained, part-based reasoning with provenance verification.

The benchmark demonstrates strong empirical validity: results show a large spread between no-search (0-15%) and full-rollout (up to 36%) performance, and adversarial filtering against multiple closed-source models suggests the tasks are not trivially solvable by parametric knowledge alone, achieving the intended difficulty.

Comprehensive evaluation across search modes (no search, single image search, full rollout) and multiple frontier and open-source models, with category and difficulty breakdowns, gives good insight into where and why models fail.

The error analysis and rollout trajectory statistics (search call distributions, verbosity vs. correctness, tool-call failures for Qwen) provide useful diagnostic insight beyond simple accuracy numbers, and the qualitative case studies (Figure 6) are illustrative and concrete.

Reasonable positioning against concurrent/related work (BrowseComp-VL, MM-BrowseComp), with an explicit discussion of how this benchmark differs (sparse localized visual cues vs. single dominant entity).
weaknesses: The benchmark size is quite small (311 tasks), which may limit statistical robustness of category-level breakdowns (some categories like Music have only 17 items) and generalizability of conclusions.

The dataset construction process is fairly manual and subjective (annotators manually selecting keyframes, judging 'suitability', and applying adversarial filtering by testing against 2 closed-source models), raising concerns about selection bias, reproducibility, and potential annotator-introduced difficulty skew rather than a principled/automatic definition of difficulty.

Only one open-source model (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B) is evaluated, which is a narrow basis for claims about 'open vs. closed' model gaps; more open-source agents (e.g., WebSailor-style or other multimodal agents) would strengthen the comparison.

The LLM-as-judge evaluation protocol’s validation is described only briefly ('complete agreement' in manual inspection) without reporting sample size, inter-annotator agreement statistics, or edge cases, weakening confidence in evaluation reliability at scale.

Cropping/grounding-based tools are mentioned as supported but not used in main experiments because they 'deteriorate performance'—this is an interesting but under-explored finding; the paper doesn't provide quantitative results for this ablation, weakening the paper's claims about the importance of fine-grained visual grounding.

Data licensing/ethical concerns around using YouTube/Bilibili video frames and arXiv figures (e.g., potential copyright, deanonymization of people in vlogs) are only briefly touched upon; more detail on consent/PII handling would strengthen the ethical treatment.

The paper's contribution is primarily a benchmark/dataset with an evaluation framework rather than a new method, so novelty is somewhat incremental relative to BrowseComp and MMSearch, mainly reconfiguring curation criteria and data sources.

Some presentation issues: dense related work section, minor duplication between main text and appendix tables, and the abstract's specific percentage claims might be better contextualized with confidence intervals or variance across repeated runs given the small dataset size.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing multimodal browsing benchmarks (e.g., MMSearch) can often be solved via shallow image-search + nearby-text heuristics rather than genuine multimodal reasoning, and the paper's analysis of this phenomenon is a useful framing contribution.

The Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation curation idea (requiring extrapolation to out-of-image facts like event dates/venues rather than reading answers directly) is a sensible design principle for increasing genuine multimodal difficulty.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across three search modes (no search, image search, full rollout) with category- and difficulty-level breakdowns, plus trajectory statistics (search-call counts, response length) and a manually curated error taxonomy that gives some insight into failure modes (e.g., 'no relevant information found', hallucination, relevance-not-verified).

Results show a large, informative headroom between current frontier models (o3 at 36% full rollout) and open models (Qwen at 6.9%), which is useful signal for the community if the benchmark construction holds up.

Provides some transparency about framework design choices (caching, content extraction into web_info/related_info) and discusses limitations of agent-driven cropping, which is an honest negative result.
weaknesses: Benchmark is very small (311 items, only 8 primary / 43 secondary categories, with some secondary categories having only 1 example), raising concerns about statistical reliability of category-level and difficulty-level breakdowns reported to one decimal place.

Heavy overlap with concurrent/contemporaneous work: BrowseComp-VL (WebWatcher) and especially MM-BrowseComp cover very similar territory (multimodal browsing benchmarks with sparse visual cues and provenance verification). The paper's differentiation from MM-BrowseComp in particular is asserted rather than empirically demonstrated (no direct comparison of task difficulty, item overlap, or head-to-head results), weakening the novelty claim.

Evaluation is limited to only 4 models (o3, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen-2.5-VL-72B), with GPT-5 missing full-rollout results entirely and no other open-source/mid-size models tested; this is a thin evaluation for a benchmark paper meant to be a 'common yardstick'.

The difficulty labeling procedure ('Easy' if solvable by o3 or Gemini without/with only image search, else 'Hard') is circular — it defines benchmark difficulty using the very models being evaluated, which biases reported 'hard' accuracy numbers and complicates comparison to future models.

Adversarial filtering against specific closed models (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro) to remove 'trivially solvable' questions risks overfitting the benchmark to make these particular models look bad, and may not generalize as a measure of genuine task difficulty versus idiosyncratic knowledge gaps of the filtering models.

LLM-as-judge validation is reported only qualitatively ('complete agreement' with human judgment) without quantitative agreement statistics (e.g., Cohen's kappa, sample size, or confusion matrix), undermining confidence in the evaluation metric's reliability.

Reliance on a single commercial search backend (SerpApi) with cached results raises reproducibility concerns if the API changes or access is unavailable to other researchers, despite claims of stability.

No human performance baseline is actually reported (Table 5 lists 'Human' with empty dashes), despite the paper repeatedly motivating the benchmark via comparison to human-level task difficulty (BrowseComp-style).

Data sources (YouTube, Bilibili, ArXiv) and categories (geography, sports, academic, film/TV, tech, games, vlog, music) are fairly narrow and skew toward entertainment/pop-culture content, which may limit generalizability of conclusions about 'multimodal browsing' broadly.

The error analysis and trajectory statistics are conducted on only one or two models (Gemini-2.5-Pro, o3) rather than uniformly across all evaluated models, limiting the generality of the qualitative conclusions.

Writing and presentation have rough edges, e.g., inconsistent definitions of 'MMSEARCH+' vs 'MMSearch-Plus', some analysis claims (e.g., Qwen's invalid tool calls) presented without clear methodology for how they were detected or verified.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated gap: existing multimodal browsing benchmarks (e.g., MMSearch) can be solved via shallow image-search + text matching without genuine fine-grained visual reasoning; the paper clearly articulates this critique with supporting evidence (e.g., GPT-4o's high scores on MMSearch vs. near-zero on BrowseComp-style tasks).

The Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation curation methodology is a thoughtful and fairly principled design choice (seeding questions on spatial/temporal cues whose answers are not directly visible), and is paired with an adversarial filtering procedure (cross-validation across models, image/text perturbation, iterative refinement) that helps ensure the benchmark isn't trivially solvable by parametric knowledge.

Results are informative and show substantial headroom for even frontier models (e.g., o3 36.0% full rollout, Qwen 0.0% without search), supporting the claim that the benchmark is meaningfully harder than prior multimodal search benchmarks.

The paper goes beyond headline accuracy with a reasonably deep analysis: rollout trajectory statistics (calls vs. correctness, verbosity), a manually curated error taxonomy with concrete case studies (Figure 6), and observations about tool-use failures (e.g., Qwen's invalid tool calls).

Reasonably thorough related-work positioning and a comparison table (Table 2) distinguishing this benchmark from concurrent works (BrowseComp-VL/WebWatcher, MM-BrowseComp) along meaningful axes (multi-hop depth, thinking-with-images, multi-image).
weaknesses: The benchmark is quite small (311 tasks), and only one open-source model (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B) is evaluated; broader open-source coverage (e.g., other VLMs, agentic frameworks like WebSailor/WebWatcher adapted to multimodal) would strengthen claims about generality of the findings versus idiosyncrasies of specific models/frameworks.

No human performance baseline is reported (the table lists 'Human' with empty values), which is a significant gap for a benchmark claiming to test genuinely hard multimodal reasoning—without it, it's hard to calibrate how 'solvable' the benchmark actually is in principle.

Evaluation relies on a single run per model/mode with no reported variance, and LLM-as-judge validation is described only briefly ('complete agreement' with manual inspection) without quantitative inter-rater statistics or sample size for this validation.

Potential data/temporal leakage concerns: although the authors filter for novelty, data sourced from YouTube/Bilibili/arXiv could still overlap with training corpora of some models over time, and the static benchmark may face increasing contamination risk as models are retrained on newer web data—this is not deeply discussed.

The error taxonomy and several reported statistics (Figure 7, Table 13) are based on manual annotation by the authors themselves with a single dominant label per error, raising concerns about subjectivity/bias in error categorization, and this is conducted only on Gemini-2.5-Pro, limiting generalizability of the error analysis across models.

The search agent framework's design choices (e.g., capped rounds, caching, top-K summaries) are reasonable but could materially affect reported accuracy numbers (especially 'Full Rollout'), and limited ablations are provided isolating the impact of these specific framework choices versus genuine model capability.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated benchmark (MMSearch-Plus) that targets a genuine gap: existing multimodal browsing benchmarks can often be solved via text-only heuristics or coarse image search without requiring sustained, fine-grained visual reasoning.

The Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation curation methodology is a thoughtful and reasonably novel design principle for constructing hard multimodal questions that require synthesizing localized visual cues with external retrieval, rather than simple entity matching.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple closed- and open-source MLLMs (o3, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen2.5-VL-72B) and five distinct search-mode configurations (no search, image search, text search, full rollout, full rollout+SoM), showing consistent and interpretable trends (e.g., substantial headroom, SoM gains).

Rich, detailed analysis section: stepwise tool-usage heatmaps, Markov transition matrices between tool types, zoom-in behavior distributions, error taxonomy with quantified failure categories, and qualitative case studies, which together provide genuine insight into agent behavior rather than just aggregate accuracy numbers.

The MMSearch+_lite subset control (removing tasks solvable via internal knowledge) is a good methodological step to disentangle parametric memorization from genuine retrieval-driven reasoning, strengthening the validity of benchmark conclusions.

Reasonably thorough ethics and reproducibility statements, including data redaction procedures, licensing considerations, and partial supplementary release; comparison table against prior benchmarks (Table 2) clearly situates the contribution relative to related work.
Human baseline included for comparison, providing useful context for interpreting model performance (though humans do not dominate across all categories, which itself is an interesting finding).
weaknesses: Dataset scale is fairly small (311 tasks, 279 unique questions), which is modest relative to typical benchmark papers at top venues; this limits statistical robustness of fine-grained category-level and difficulty-level breakdowns (many categories have very few examples, e.g., Vlog with 19 images, Music with 17).

The benchmark's construction relies heavily on filtering questions that specific closed-source models (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, o3) can or cannot solve, which risks overfitting the benchmark's difficulty profile to the idiosyncrasies of these particular models rather than measuring a more general notion of 'genuine multimodal reasoning'; the paper acknowledges 'dataset updates' are needed due to temporal drift, underscoring this fragility.

Reliance on a single closed-source LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o) for answer correctness, with validation limited to a subset consistency check against Gemini-2.5-Pro; no human-judgment agreement statistics (e.g., Cohen's kappa) are reported beyond a claim of 'complete agreement,' which is somewhat underspecified.

The Set-of-Mark (SoM) module depends on human-curated bounding boxes rather than automatic detection, which is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation; this makes the 'agentic' SoM pathway less representative of a fully autonomous deployment scenario, since real-world agents would need to localize regions themselves.

The gains from SoM are relatively modest and inconsistent (e.g., +1.6 for o3, +3.9 for Gemini, +1.0 for Qwen in Table 1), and the paper's own analysis shows performance can regress under full rollout for the 'easy' split, which somewhat undercuts the narrative that the proposed framework straightforwardly improves multimodal reasoning.

Some methodological choices are not fully justified: e.g., why text search is capped at 20 rounds while other settings differ, why Qwen's image-search cap differs (10 vs 20) based on a pilot study without reporting that pilot's results, and the somewhat ad hoc labeling of 'easy' vs 'difficult' derived post hoc from specific models' performance.

The related-work distinction from concurrent contemporaneous benchmarks (MM-BrowseComp, BrowseComp-VL) is argued primarily through curation methodology (spatial-temporal extrapolation) and Table 2 feature checklist, but the paper does not include direct empirical comparison (e.g., running the same models on MM-BrowseComp side-by-side) to substantiate the claimed unique difficulty/insight contribution.

Appendices are very large and some analyses (e.g., Figure 15 rollout trajectory statistics) are described but not deeply interpreted in the main text, suggesting the empirical narrative could be tightened and better integrated rather than relegated to extensive appendices.

No open-source release of the full dataset is confirmed (only a 30-example random subset was uploaded due to size constraints), which somewhat limits the reproducibility of the full benchmark evaluation at submission time.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine gap in existing multimodal browsing benchmarks (e.g., MMSearch), namely that many tasks can be solved via text-only shortcuts without real visual reasoning, and proposes a well-motivated curation principle (Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation) that seeds questions requiring extrapolation from localized visual cues to out-of-image facts.

The empirical results convincingly show substantial headroom: even the strongest tested system (o3) achieves only 36-37.6% end-to-end accuracy, and the benchmark resists trivial parametric shortcuts (0% no-search accuracy for the open-source model), supporting the claim of genuine difficulty.

The paper provides an unusually thorough behavioral analysis: stepwise tool-usage heatmaps, Markov tool-transition probabilities, zoom-in frequency distributions, and a manually curated error taxonomy, offering useful diagnostic insight into how/why current agents fail (e.g., 'no relevant information found' as the dominant error, OCR-vs-image-search preferences).

The proposed Set-of-Mark (SoM) zoom-in module is a practical, model-agnostic extension that yields consistent (if modest) accuracy gains across multiple closed- and open-source models, and the paper includes ablations isolating its effect (Full Rollout vs. Full Rollout+SoM) as well as a 'lite' subset (MMSearch+_lite) to control for models' internal knowledge.
Extensive appendix material (case studies, full agent trajectories, prompts, dataset statistics, comparison table against prior benchmarks) supports transparency and partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The benchmark is fairly small (311 tasks, 8 primary categories, some categories with as few as 17-19 examples such as Vlog/Music), which raises concerns about statistical reliability of per-category accuracy numbers and the generality of conclusions drawn from them.

The adversarial filtering procedure removes questions solvable by the very same frontier models (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, o3) that are later used as evaluation subjects/judges, creating a degree of circularity: the benchmark is explicitly tuned to be hard for the models being benchmarked, which could inflate apparent difficulty and complicate fair comparison with future or different models.

The 'Easy vs. Hard' difficulty labeling is defined post-hoc based on whether o3/Gemini-2.5-Pro could solve the item without or with only image search, which is a model-dependent (and somewhat circular) definition of difficulty rather than an independent criterion.

Novelty relative to concurrent, closely related benchmarks (MM-BrowseComp, BrowseComp-VL) is somewhat thin; the differentiation is described qualitatively ('data sources' and 'framework emphasis') without a quantitative demonstration that MMSearch-Plus meaningfully advances beyond these concurrent efforts on the specific dimensions claimed (e.g., fine-grained visual reasoning).

The gains from the paper's main technical contribution (SoM zoom-in) are modest (+1.6 to +3.9 accuracy points across models), and for GPT-5 and Qwen the reported settings are incomplete/inconsistent (e.g., GPT-5's Image Search row alone, missing Full Rollout without SoM in Table 1), making it hard to fully assess SoM's isolated contribution.

LLM-as-judge validation is described vaguely ('manual inspection showed complete agreement') without reporting sample size, inter-rater agreement statistics, or a systematic protocol, which weakens confidence in the accuracy metric's reliability.

The benchmark depends on live, third-party web content (via SerpAPI and general video/paper sources) that can change or disappear over time; the authors acknowledge unavoidable 'temporal drift' and the need for 'regular refreshing,' which undermines long-term reproducibility and stable cross-paper comparison.

Human baseline evaluation appears to involve limited annotator resources (browsing capped at 10-20 minutes, unclear number of annotators), and the human accuracy (22.8%) is reported without variance or discussion of annotator skill/tool familiarity, limiting the reliability of human-vs-model comparisons.
No compute/cost accounting is provided for the up to 20-round agentic rollouts, which is relevant given the practical cost of reproducing or scaling this evaluation protocol.
The full dataset itself is not released (only a 30-example anonymized subset), which limits independent verification of the benchmark's overall statistics and difficulty claims during review.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated gap: existing multimodal browsing benchmarks often collapse to a narrow form of image-source cross-validation that can be solved by text-only heuristics, whereas MMSearch-Plus explicitly targets fine-grained, sustained visual reasoning.

The Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation curation methodology (requiring extrapolation to out-of-image facts via localized spatial/temporal cues) is a thoughtful and non-trivial design principle for constructing hard multimodal tasks, and the adversarial filtering procedure (cross-validation against multiple closed-source models, image perturbation, iterative refinement) demonstrates care in ensuring genuine retrieval-dependence.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning closed-source (o3, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro) and open-source (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) models across five search modes, plus a 'lite' subset (MMSearch-Plus_lite) that controls for models' parametric knowledge, strengthening the internal validity of the conclusions.
The Set-of-Mark (SoM) zoom-in module is a useful, general contribution that enables 'thinking with images' behavior analysis and yields measurable, consistent accuracy gains across models.

Extensive and genuinely insightful analysis: stepwise tool-use heatmaps, Markov transition matrices between tool types, zoom-in frequency distributions, a manually curated error taxonomy, and detailed qualitative case studies (both failure and success trajectories) that shed light on why and how models fail.

Reasonable reproducibility effort: prompts, framework details, dataset subset, and an anonymized code/data archive are provided, and the appendix is unusually thorough (18 pages) with transparent documentation of design choices.
weaknesses: The benchmark is fairly small (311 tasks, 279 unique questions across 8 primary/43 secondary categories), so per-category breakdowns (e.g., only 17 Music or 19 Vlog examples) may be too noisy to support some of the fine-grained claims (e.g., category-specific benefit of image vs. text search), and no variance/confidence intervals or repeated-run statistics are reported for the inherently stochastic MLLM outputs.

There is a degree of circularity in the dataset construction: the adversarial filtering step explicitly uses the same or highly similar frontier models (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, o3) that are later used as the primary evaluated systems and as the LLM-judge, which risks the benchmark being tailored to current weaknesses of these specific models rather than measuring a more model-agnostic notion of difficulty; the paper's own acknowledgment that some items 'became solvable' over time and require periodic refreshing underscores this fragility.

Evaluation relies on LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o) with only a brief mention of manual validation ('complete agreement' on an unspecified sample size); more detail on judge validation (sample size, inter-annotator agreement, disagreement cases) would strengthen confidence in the reported accuracy numbers.

Only one open-source model (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) is evaluated, and no other recent open-source or specialized agentic search systems mentioned extensively in the related work (e.g., WebSailor, WebWatcher, DeepEyes, Search-R1-style RL agents) are empirically benchmarked, limiting insight into how the difficulty pattern generalizes beyond a narrow set of proprietary frontier models plus one open model.

The agent framework's reliance on MLLM-generated webpage summaries (web_info/related_info, generated by Gemini) as the interface to retrieved content, rather than raw page content, could introduce a confound: retrieval quality is partly gated by an auxiliary model's summarization ability, which is not separately ablated or validated, and may bias comparisons for models whose failure could stem from summary quality rather than search/reasoning ability itself.

The human baseline (10–20 minutes per task with a standard browser) is a fairly narrow experimental setup and may underestimate achievable human performance, making some of the human-vs-model comparisons (e.g., in Sports/Vlog) less conclusive than presented.

Despite claiming closeness in difficulty profile to BrowseComp-like text benchmarks, there is no direct quantitative comparison table against concurrent, closely related multimodal benchmarks (MM-BrowseComp, BrowseComp-VL) beyond qualitative discussion in the appendix, so the paper's claimed advantages over these concurrent works remain only partially substantiated empirically.
